statement: Guarantee access to food, clothing, housing, education and healthcare

summary.why: The Progressive Party says economic and political power should serve people rather than concentrated wealth (its stated philosophy draws on economic democracy and 'neohumanism').
summary.how: Listed in the health, housing and education sections as guarantees for everyone.

statement: Create an independent National Health Board outside the Health Ministry to oversee Te Whatu Ora

summary.why: The party says this would counterbalance political influence on health priorities.
summary.how: A board of health experts with elected and appointed members, plus co-operative primary and residential care, Māori-for-Māori services and higher taxes on harmful products ring-fenced for health.

statement: Legalise cannabis as a health issue and support the End-of-Life Choice Act

summary.how: Tax revenue from cannabis would go to health, with research on benefits and harms; the party also lists voluntary vaccination and a review of Covid-era measures for future pandemics.

statement: Offer state-funded mortgages, a state-owned house-building enterprise and limit home ownership to NZ residents

summary.why: The party says leaving housing to the market 'amounts to a dereliction of duty'.
summary.how: Also long-term leasing, co-operative housing and co-housing options, and a capital gains tax to curb speculation.

statement: Make te reo Māori compulsory in primary and secondary schools, aiming for a bilingual Aotearoa

summary.how: Language parity with English, plus full teaching of New Zealand history and the constitutional documents (Te Tiriti and He Whakaputanga).

statement: Entrench the Māori seats in Parliament

summary.how: Give the Māori seats the same entrenched protection as general seats.

statement: Move schooling from national standards to child-centred, experiential learning including meditation and mindfulness

summary.how: Learning based on each child's needs, parents as active partners, restorative behaviour management and a Hauora (holistic wellbeing) approach.

statement: Focus prisons on rehabilitation, education and restorative justice, and end for-profit prisons

summary.why: The party views crime as rooted in social and economic conditions.
summary.how: Skills training and tikanga Māori in prisons, mental-health services, restorative justice, community reintegration support, and terminating private prison arrangements.

statement: Establish a Ministry for Animal and Plant Welfare and extend legal advocacy to nature

summary.how: Building on Te Urewera's legal personhood and animals' legal recognition as sentient.

statement: Shift farming to co-operatives and plant-based protein

summary.how: Incentivise farmers to move to plant protein (including lab-grown meat) and regenerative, ethical farming models; co-operatives at all levels of agriculture.

statement: Build a government-backed renewables industry and prepare to move infrastructure 10 metres above sea level

summary.how: Electrify transport, convert sewage and organic waste to biogas and biodiesel, raise eco-housing standards, phase out gas appliances, and redirect foreign aid toward emissions cuts in the Pacific.

statement: Run businesses with more than nine employees as worker co-operatives and state-manage monopolistic key industries

summary.how: A Minister, Ministry and Centre for Cooperative Studies; railways, power and mining state-managed; a nationwide co-operative supermarket to cut living costs.

statement: Phase out income tax in favour of taxes on production, remove GST from fresh produce and introduce a capital gains tax

summary.how: Income tax would become a mechanism capping salaries at a maximum linked to the minimum wage, set by a Wages and Salary Commission.

statement: Create Social Boards of respected community members to advise local and national government

summary.why: The party says they would moderate lobby groups' influence.
